newsitem.title: USA: Four firms sue ADM over citric acid pricing.
newsitem.headline: Four firms sue ADM over citric acid pricing.

text.p: Four companies have sued Archer Daniels Midland Co. and other producers of citric acid, seeking triple damages for allegedly charging prices that were inflated by an antitrust scheme.
The lawsuit was filed Monday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco by Procter & Gamble Co.; Kraft Foods Inc., a unit of Philip Morris Cos. Inc.; Quaker Oats Co.; and Schreiber Foods Inc.
The defendants in the lawsuit, including ADM, have previously agreed to pay criminal fines in a U.S. antitrust probe.
ADM declined to comment on the lawsuit.

Besides ADM, defendants named in the suit are Haarman & Reimer Corp, a subsidiary of Bayer AG; Hoffman-LaRoche Inc. and F. Hoffman-LaRoche Ltd., which are part of Roche Holding Ltd.; SA Citrique Belge NV; and Jungbunzlauer Inc. and Jungbunzlauer International AG of Switzerland.

The lawsuit was filed by the four companies who previously opted out of a civil class-action settlement. As part of that settlement, ADM agreed to pay $35 million to settle citric acid price litigation.
In court documents, the plaintiffs charge the defendants with conspiring to fix prices of citric acid.

The plaintiffs said they are among the largest U.S. purchasers of citric acid, an additive made from fermented corn. The companies said that, for the period from 1991 through 1995, they bought more than $350 million worth of citric acid from the defendants and other suppliers.

Because of the alleged price-fixing scheme, the plaintiffs said they paid more for the product than they otherwise would have paid. As a result, they said, they suffered an undetermined amount of damages.
Last year, ADM pleaded guilty to two counts of fixing prices of citric acid and lysine, a feed additive, and agreed to pay $100 million in fines to the U.S. Justice Department.
In addition, Hoffman-LaRoche agreed to pay $14 million in U.S. criminal fines, Jungbunzlauer agreed to $11 million, and Haarman & Reimer agreed to $50 million in fines.
Citric acid, a $1.2 billion worldwide market, is used in soft drinks, processed foods, detergents, textiles, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.
